item.title: Approximate Counting and the Provability of Combinatorial Principles
item.description: arXiv:2611.33356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding which axioms suffice for the provability of known results in algorithms and complexity and whether they can settle longstanding conjectures in these areas is a fundamental direction at the intersection of logic and computer science. Motivated by this research program and its applications, we investigate bounded arithmetic theories designed to serve as a logical foundation for *probabilistic reasoning*, the relation between these theories, and whether they can prove more theorems than their underlying base theory for *deterministic reasoning*. In more detail, for nearly twenty years, Je\v{r}\'abek's theory $\mathsf{APC}_1$ [Je\v{r}07a] has provided a standard framework for the formalization of results from theoretical computer science relying on probabilistic techniques. In a recent work, [CLOW26] introduced a (possibly weaker) theory called $\mathsf{APX}_1$. This theory is able to capture a large set of probabilistic arguments using four simple axioms for *approximate counting*. Both theories extend Cook's theory $\mathsf{PV}_1$ [Coo75] for deterministic polynomial-time reasoning. Our main result establishes that, in the relativized setting, $\mathsf{APX}_1$ does not prove the retraction weak pigeonhole principle ($\mathsf{rwPHP}$). Consequently, $\mathsf{APC}_1$ is not conservative over $\mathsf{APX}_1$ with respect to relativized $\forall\Sigma^b_1$ sentences. Moreover, we establish that the unprovability of $\mathsf{rwPHP}$ is part of a more general phenomenon: for a large class of finite combinatorial principles, the existence of an *infinite model* of the negation of the principle *characterizes* its unprovability in $\mathsf{APX}_1$. This result, which is analogous to a theorem of Riis [Rii94], implies that $\mathsf{PV}_1$ and $\mathsf{APX}_1$ prove exactly the same finite combinatorial principles of this form.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Korten, Jiatu Li, Igor C. Oliveira, Hanlin Ren

item.title: Higher-Dimensional Automata in Geometric Logic
item.description: arXiv:2611.33838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What does the topos of a higher-dimensional automaton know about its infinite behaviour that its language does not? We write partial HDAs with an infinite run as models of a geometric theory over an intuitionistic metatheory with no choice. The topos of a machine is that of sheaves on its prefixes. The label word of a prefix records the shape and acceptance bit of each cell with the ipomset of each step. Under unique choice these words give a geometric morphism to the label topos of sheaves on label words, which thus records the shapes and acceptance bits that the B\"uchi language forgets. Machines sharing their B\"uchi language and their frames can differ over the label topos. The bouquet of two squares shares its frame and its B\"uchi language with the interleaved square; each accepted run of either reads the two events in parallel forever. Only the interleaved square has runs through cells of shape a, and the geometric sequent excluding such runs separates the two over the label topos. Over alphabets with decidable equality, finite rigid machines are unambiguous exactly when their label maps are inclusions of locales, and their equivalence over the label topos is decided whenever either is unambiguous. Equivalences of frames over the label topos transport points with their labels, and the invariants of fibres and of the language of points follow from this transport. On finite partial HDAs over alphabets with decidable equality, Muller and B\"uchi acceptance coincide exactly under a weak form of excluded middle.
item.dc:creator: Kenan Oggad

item.title: Direct cognition problem: a semantic skeleton of mathematics and its growth
item.description: arXiv:2611.34210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a finite semantic skeleton from three axioms of classical propositional logic without specifying a target theorem. During growth, the constructor records which proofs share an intermediate lemma. When choosing the final anchors, it also counts inferences that use a premise the lemma can supply by substitution. The primary skeleton contains ten anchors whose certificates expand to the axioms through 27 shared inference steps. It shortens all 30 previously unseen proof structures in an external catalogue of typed combinators, saving 90 of 412 steps. One anchor recurs in all five runs of the constructor. In a post hoc test, this anchor alone shortens 26 of the 30 proofs. It also shortens 331 of 475 previously unseen proofs of familiar theorems in a second corpus.
item.dc:creator: Vasilii A. Gromov, Nikolai N. Evdokimov

item.title: A Complete Axiomatisation of Distribution-Based Branching Bisimilarity for Non-Deterministic and Probabilistic Choice
item.description: arXiv:2611.34311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a notion of branching bisimilarity for non-deterministic probabilistic processes. In order to characterise the corresponding notion of rooted branching probabilistic bisimilarity, an equational theory is proposed for a basic, recursion-free process language with non-deterministic as well as probabilistic choice. The proof of completeness of the axiomatisation builds on the completeness of strong probabilistic bisimilarity on the one hand and on the notion of a concrete process, i.e. a process that does not display (partially) inert {\tau}-moves, on the other hand. The approach is first presented for the non-deterministic fragment of the calculus and next generalised to incorporate probabilistic choice, too.
item.dc:creator: Rob J. van Glabbeek, Jan Friso Groote, Erik P. de Vink

item.title: Higher-Order Generation of First-Order Theories
item.description: arXiv:2611.34714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a logic whose formulae are finite descriptions of possibly infinite first-order theories. A theory is a set of first-order sentences, generated in our setting by a higher-order recursion scheme. Such a scheme is a finite grammar whose parameters may denote trees or operations on trees. We consider two interpretations: a model must satisfy every generated sentence under the conjunctive interpretation, and at least one under the disjunctive interpretation. For schemes of order $k=0$, these theories coincide with the regular first-order theories of Mathur et al. (POPL 2025). We generalize this representation by allowing higher-order schemes, while retaining first-order quantification in every generated sentence. We study the expressive power, model checking, and satisfiability of this logic. Over finite ordered structures, we show that disjunctive theories of existential sentences generated at order at most $k$ capture $k$-EXPTIME, for every $k\geq0$. Allowing unrestricted first-order sentences captures $(k+1)$-EXPTIME at the same scheme order, where $0$-EXPTIME denotes polynomial time. We also give model-checking algorithms in the corresponding time classes for each fixed signature, variable-name set, and order bound. For satisfiability under either interpretation, we extend several decidability results for regular theories to every order. However, we show that conjunctive satisfiability of quantifier-free theories, decidable at order zero, becomes undecidable already at order one. Finally, we recover decidable conjunctive satisfiability at every order by separating higher-order generation of Boolean structure from independent regular generation of ground atoms. Together, these results show how higher-order generation of first-order syntax captures the exponential-time hierarchy while retaining decidable satisfiability in restricted fragments.
item.dc:creator: Ziyue Jin, Umang Mathur

item.title: Translation Validation of SystemVerilog-to-SystemC RTL Conversion by Reading the Generated C++
item.description: arXiv:2611.31674v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: SystemC models of register-transfer level (RTL) designs are used for virtual platforms, firmware bring-up and simulation without a commercial license, and more of them now come from translators and language models. A wrong model usually compiles, and it usually agrees with the RTL. SystemVerilog evaluates an 8-bit sum in 8 bits while C++ evaluates it in 64, so a translation that forgets one truncation keeps a carry the RTL drops, and only inputs near the top of the range show it. I built svcc, an open-source SystemVerilog-to-SystemC converter, and my first check of its output read the generated C++ with SystemVerilog's rules. That check passed two wrong models. The check that replaced it gives the generated header the meaning C++17 and SystemC give it and turns undefined behavior into proof obligations. It prints what it read as SystemVerilog with every width change explicit, then proves that equivalent to a netlist of the source by induction over registers matched by name. On 50 author-written designs it proves 45 and reports 5 as outside its model. In a mutation experiment it accepted none of the 17 mutants that compiled SystemC showed to be wrong. Of 2,184 modules from 16 open-source code bases, 1,185 conversions match Verilator in random co-simulation and the check proves 600 of them. The same runs found defects in the front end, in svcc and in Verilator.
item.dc:creator: Mayur Kubavat

item.title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.33303v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof. A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.
item.dc:creator: Baptiste Juran, Dimitri Kachler, Damien Sileo

item.title: Algebraic Diversity of Switching Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.33938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Algebraic Diversity generalizes averaging over many observations to averaging one observation over a group of transformations matched to its structure. This paper develops the framework on the Boolean cube $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ for the translations, the coordinate permutations, the hyperoctahedral group, and the general linear and affine groups. It determines the commutant of each action and gives closed forms for the group-averaged second-order statistic of one truth table, which collapses to the Walsh periodogram for the translations, to per-weight averages for the hyperoctahedral group, and to the weight up to complementation for the affine group. Bent functions are exactly those whose translation average is white, the Haar transform along an input order is the multiplexer tree of Shannon's expansion, and higher-order averages see only the weight below a first informative order, two for the translations and four for the affine group. A matched stabilizer stands in for repeated observations, since a vote over orbits of $s$ points divides by $s$ the number of noisy truth tables a target error requires. The same viewpoint gives the affine hull of a function as matched coordinates, an exact variance identity for XOR hashing, and matched hashes whose variance never exceeds that of a pairwise independent hash. Applications on public benchmarks include hash choice for approximate model counting, the decision of parity-structured formulas and the refutation of counting formulas modulo 3 and 4 from the spectra of clause blocks, separation of NPN classes by canonical spectra, tested on ISCAS-85 cut functions and all five-input classes, correction of noisy truth tables and protection of lookup tables by voting over symmetries, blind group matching, and an analog of the CLEAN algorithm that writes a truth table as the XOR of atoms in the fixed spaces of groups. All proofs are given in full.
item.dc:creator: Mitchell A. Thornton

item.title: The Equational Theory of Rational String-to-String Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.34324v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a sound and complete equational axiomatisation of the rational string-to-string functions, which can be seen as a transducer counterpart of the classical axiomatisations of regular languages by Salomaa [JACM'66], Krob [TCS'91], Bloom and \'Esik [MSCS'93], and Kozen [IC'94]. The axioms are stated over a compositional, algebraic syntax for rational functions, namely the rational fragment of the syntax for regular functions introduced by Boja\'nczyk, Daviaud and Krishna [LICS'18]. The axiomatisation is finitary, as it consists of finitely many uniform families of axioms, each parameterised by the types involved. It is also purely equational: it consists only of equations, with no implication rules.
item.dc:creator: Miko{\l}aj Boja\'nczyk, Kacper Lewandowski, Katzper Michno

item.title: Higher rewriting for strong linearly distributive coherence
item.description: arXiv:2611.34596v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rewriting is a computational method to solve word problems: deciding whether two compound expressions, or words, are equivalent with respect to a set of identities. Higher rewriting generalizes rewriting to higher-dimensional words, or cells, in higher categories. Following Guiraud and Malbos, we use higher rewriting to generalize Mac Lane's coherence theorem. Our result concerns strong linearly distributive categories: categories equipped with two unital tensor products related by invertible distributors. We show that in a strong linearly distributive category every formal diagram commutes.
item.dc:creator: Max Demirdilek, Christian Reiher, Christoph Schweigert

item.title: Propositional Dynamic Logic has Craig Interpolation: a tableau-based proof
item.description:
arXiv:2503.13276v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that Propositional Dynamic Logic (PDL) has the Craig Interpolation Property. This question has been open for many years. Three proof attempts were published, but later criticized in the literature or retracted. Our proof is based on the main ideas from Borzechowski (1988, master thesis). We define a cyclic tableau system for PDL with a loading mechanism to recognize successful repeats. For this system, we show soundness and completeness via a game.
To show interpolation, we modify Maehara's method to work for tableaux with repeats: we first define pre-interpolants at each node, and then use a quasi-tableau to define interpolants for clusters (strongly connected components). In different terms, our method solves the fixpoint equations that characterize the desired interpolants, and the method ensures that the solutions to these equations can be expressed within PDL.
The proof is constructive and we show how to compute interpolants. We make available a Haskell implementation of the proof system that provides interpolants, and a formal verification of our proof in the interactive theorem prover Lean. Lastly, we discuss several questions for future work.
item.dc:creator: Manfred Borzechowski, Malvin Gattinger, Helle Hvid Hansen, Revantha Ramanayake, Francisco Trucco Dalmas, Yde Venema

item.title: interwhen: A Generalizable Framework for Steering Reasoning Models with Test-time Verification
item.description: arXiv:2602.11202v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning models produce long traces of intermediate decisions and tool calls, making test-time verification important for ensuring correctness. Existing approaches either verify only the final answer, which misses early errors, or rely on branch-and-verify strategies that explore multiple trajectories. We introduce interwhen, a single-trajectory verification framework that steers model behavior by providing feedback on intermediate reasoning traces. It addresses two key challenges. First, given a set of verifiers, obtaining verifiable states from the reasoning trace typically requires prompt engineering or external task decomposition into fixed steps. Instead, we propose a monitoring system that periodically polls the reasoning trace and forks inference of the reasoning model to recover intermediate states. Verifiers are run asynchronously alongside generation, adding negligible overhead on correct executions and intervening only when violations occur. Second, beyond math and code, a central challenge for process verification is the scarcity of verifiers. interwhen addresses this through automatic verifier synthesis from natural-language policy documents. Given a policy, it can generate code-based verifiers, including provably correct verifiers in Lean and z3. Together, these contributions yield a plug-and-play test-time verification system that can improve task completion and policy compliance of any reasoning agent. On reasoning benchmarks where policies encode mathematical or logical constraints, interwhen achieves near-perfect accuracy for reasoning models using a fraction of the tokens of baselines. On agentic benchmarks with policy-based verifier generation, it enables improvements in task quality for SLMs without any finetuning, e.g., task completion rate of Qwen3-30B jumps from 32% to 87% on the telecom domain in tau2-bench. Code at https://github.com/microsoft/interwhen.
item.dc:creator: Vishak K Bhat, Vijval Ekbote, Prateek Chanda, Ashmit Khandelwal, Maitreyi Swaroop, Vineeth N. Balasubramanian, Subbarao Kambhampati, Nagarajan Natarajan, Amit Sharma

item.title: Parameterized Enumeration of Minimal Defensive Alliances
item.description: arXiv:2609.27984v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we consider the complexity of enumerating inclusion minimal defensive alliances. We present a polynomial-delay algorithm on graphs with maximum degree 5. We complement this result by proving that there is no output-polynomial algorithm on bipartite graphs with maximum degree 6 and degeneracy 2, unless P = NP. Furthermore, there is an \FPT-delay algorithm when parameterized by neighborhood diversity. This result is the first exploit of a recently published enumeration algorithm for ILPs. By way in contrast, we prove that, for the parameter pathwidth, there is no FPT-delay algorithm for enumerating all inclusion minimal defensive alliances (unless FPT = W[1]). This is the first non-enumerability result using parameterized complexity for variations of Another/Next-problems.
item.dc:creator: Henning Fernau, Kevin Mann, Arne Meier, Heribert Vollmer

item.title: The Density of Interpolants in Modal Logic: First Results
item.description: arXiv:2611.26091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We initiate a quantitative study of interpolation in propositional modal logic. Instead of asking only whether a logic has Craig or uniform interpolation, we measure the density of formulas, or pairs of formulas, admitting interpolants. For quasi-normal modal logics, formulas of bounded modal depth over finite signatures are counted modulo logical equivalence. We show that interpolation failure is local to cells determined by the retained signature, yielding product decompositions of both uniform and Craig interpolation densities. These decompositions allow us to analyse their asymptotic behaviour as either the retained or the forgotten signature grows. When the retained signature grows, we obtain general results for all quasi-normal modal logics; when the forgotten signature grows, the behaviour is subtler, particularly when formulas are counted after existential quantification over forgotten variables. For locally tabular logics, we introduce cell incompatibility graphs and use them for a fine-grained analysis covering tabular logics, the difference logic Diff, and bounded-depth extensions of Grz.
item.dc:creator: Roman Kontchakov, Louwe Kuijer, Frank Wolter

item.title: Littlestone Dimension and Its Dual
item.description: arXiv:2611.26721v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The dual Littlestone dimension of a concept class $\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$, $\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H}):=\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H}^*)$, is the Littlestone dimension of the dual class $\mathcal{H}^*$, obtained by exchanging the roles of domain points and hypotheses. A classical result of Shelah implies that $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})$ and $\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H})$ are finite simultaneously, and quantitative results of Hodges [Mathematika, 1981] imply the doubly exponential bound $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\le 2^{2^{O(\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H}))}}$. Malliaris and Moran [Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 2024] asked whether this bound is optimal. We answer this by proving the bound \[ \operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\le 2^{O(\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H}))}, \] which is tight up to the constant in the exponent, as witnessed by the class of all binary hypotheses on a finite domain.
item.dc:creator: Pooya Hatami, Chavdar Lalov

item.title: The Uniform Functional Interpretation with Informative Types
item.description: arXiv:2508.12781v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We discuss a new approach to functional interpretations based on uniform quantification and relativization. The uniform quantification in the background permits a more penetrating analysis of principles related to collection and contra-collection. Relativization comes from a computationally informative notion of being an element of a given type. The approach is flexible. When the information takes the shape of bounds, we can recapture a form of the combination of G\"odel's functional {\em dialectica} interpretation with majorizability. When the information is "canonical" in function types, we obtain new functional interpretations and new models of G\"odel's theory T.
item.dc:creator: Fernando Ferreira, Paulo Oliva

item.title: Realizability Is Not Enough: Encoding, Liveness, and Auditing of Synthesized Robot Supervisors
item.description: arXiv:2609.30460v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-level robotic supervisors coordinate asynchronous capabilities through their reported outcomes, such as success or failure. Building on our earlier capability-based synthesis framework, we present the complete architecture, implementation, and formal foundations of an open-source pipeline for generating executable Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 Flexible Behavior Engine (FlexBE) supervisors. The pipeline integrates capability-based Generalized Reactivity (1) (GR(1)) specification generation, assumption analysis, reactive synthesis, strategy auditing, behavior-preserving state reduction, and controller realization. We evaluate enumerated and one-hot encodings and two liveness formulations in six comparisons across four domains, with additional PiHawk quadcopter flights. Under the tested backend, enumerated encoding usually synthesizes faster, although fewer propositions do not reliably predict smaller controllers or binary decision diagrams. Within the tested budget, only System-Goal without pending memory yielded executable controllers under both encodings across all six comparisons. Fair-Outcome with pending memory can yield realizable strategies that enter cycles from which the configured goal is unreachable. These failures show why realizability alone does not establish deployment readiness. The auditor checks for protocol violations, deadlocks, and goal-unreachable traps. For the tested backend and models, we recommend pairing enumerated encoding with System-Goal without pending memory and auditing each extracted strategy before realization.
item.dc:creator: David C. Conner, Joshua Luzier, William J. Doyle, Emma R. Faith, Aubrie B. Kooiker, Andrew J. Farney, Sebastian Fox, Evangelina Grimes, Ian G. Conner, Kyle Bloom
